title: Homomorphisms of abelian varieties form a finite free abelian group
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $A,B$ be abelian varieties over $k$ [def-sc-abelian-variety]. Write $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)$ for the $k$-group-scheme homomorphisms [def-sc-group-scheme], with pointwise addition induced by the group law of $B$. Then $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)$ is a free abelian group of finite rank: it has a finite $\mathbf Z$-basis [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. In particular $\operatorname{End}_k(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,A)$, with pointwise addition and multiplication given by composition, is a unital associative ring whose additive group is free of finite rank; its multiplicative identity is $\mathrm{id}_A$.

source.place: Chapter I, Theorem 10.15, printed p.49 (finite free Hom conclusion); §10 endomorphism-ring convention, printed pp.42–43.

proof.text: By [lem-sc-av-commutative], the group law of every abelian variety is commutative. Thus the pointwise sum $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ and inverse $(-f)(x)=-f(x)$ of group-scheme homomorphisms are again group-scheme homomorphisms: these maps are composites of the diagonal, $(f,g)$, and the multiplication or inverse maps, and preservation of addition is the commutative-group identity $(f(x)+g(x))+(f(y)+g(y))=(f(x)+f(y))+(g(x)+g(y))$. The group identities hold as identities of these composites. Consequently every $\operatorname{Hom}_k(X,Y)$ is an abelian group, and composition is additive in each variable.

source.place: Chapter I, §1, printed p.8, and the Hom and End conventions of §10, printed pp.42–43.

proof.text: Choose $\ell=2$ if $\operatorname{char}k\ne2$, and $\ell=3$ otherwise; in either case $\ell$ is a prime different from $\operatorname{char}k$. By [lem-sfb-abelian-tate-action-saturation], each $M=\operatorname{Hom}_k(X,Y)$ embeds additively in $H=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z_\ell}(T_\ell X,T_\ell Y)\cong\mathbf Z_\ell^{4\dim X\dim Y}$. The ring $\mathbf Z_\ell$ is contained in the characteristic-zero field $\mathbf Q_\ell$ by [def-weil-l-adic-numbers], so a nonzero integer cannot annihilate a nonzero element of $H$. Thus every such $M$ is torsion-free. In particular, for a positive-dimensional $k$-simple variety $C$, put $E=\operatorname{End}_k(C)$. By [lem-trf-torsionfree-rationalization-injective], regard $E$ as a subgroup of $E^0=E\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$. No finite-dimensionality of $E^0$ is assumed here.

source.place: Chapter I, Lemma 10.6, printed p.45; proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.49, before the choice of a rational basis.

proof.text: Let $e_1,\ldots,e_r\in E$ be any finite rationally independent family, let $V=\sum_i\mathbf Qe_i\subseteq E^0$, and let $\Lambda=E\cap V$. Use these coordinates to embed $V$ additively into $\mathbf R^r$. By [lem-sfb-abelian-degree-polynomial], the degree on $V$ is represented by a rational polynomial $P$ with $P(0)=0$. Extend its coefficients to $\mathbf R$. For $0\ne a\in\Lambda$, [lem-sfb-simple-isogeny-decomposition] says that $a:C\to C$ is an isogeny; hence $P(a)=\deg(a)$ is a positive integer. A real polynomial is continuous because it is a finite sum of finite products of continuous coordinate functions. Therefore $U=\{x:|P(x)|<1\}$ is an open neighbourhood of zero in $\mathbf R^r$ and $U\cap\Lambda=\{0\}$. Translating $U$ by any $a\in\Lambda$ shows that every singleton in $\Lambda$ is open in its subspace topology. Thus $\Lambda$ is a discrete integer submodule of $\mathbf R^r$, including the case $r=0$.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.49, degree-polynomial discreteness argument.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-discrete-real-submodule-finite] to the discrete subgroup in the previous step: $\Lambda$ is finitely generated. It is torsion-free as a subgroup of $E$, so [lem-trf-fg-torsionfree-group-free] gives a finite integer basis $b_1,\ldots,b_s$. This is a rational basis of $V$: if $\sum_j q_jb_j=0$ with $q_j\in\mathbf Q$, choose an integer $D>0$ with every $Dq_j\in\mathbf Z$. Then $\sum_j(Dq_j)b_j=0$ in $E^0$, hence in $E$ by step 2; integer independence gives $Dq_j=0$ and therefore $q_j=0$. Rational spanning follows because $\Lambda$ contains $e_1,\ldots,e_r$, which span $V$. Consequently $s=r$, and $|\Lambda/\ell\Lambda|=\ell^r$, by reducing these basis coordinates modulo $\ell$.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.49, the subgroup $\mathbf QM\cap\operatorname{End}(C)$ and the reference there to ANT 4.15.

proof.text: Write $H=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf Z_\ell}(T_\ell C)$ and $N=4(\dim C)^2$. Tate action sends $\ell\Lambda$ into $\ell H$, since $\iota(\ell b)=\ell\iota(b)$, so it defines a homomorphism $\Lambda/\ell\Lambda\to H/\ell H$. This homomorphism is injective. Indeed, if $a\in\Lambda$ maps into $\ell H$, [lem-sfb-abelian-tate-action-saturation] gives $a=\ell b$ with $b\in E$. In $E^0$ one has $b=a/\ell\in V$, so $b\in\Lambda$. This proves that the kernel is zero, and applying the same argument to differences proves injectivity. The same cited node gives $H\cong\mathbf Z_\ell^N$, and [def-weil-l-adic-numbers] gives $\mathbf Z_\ell/\ell\mathbf Z_\ell\cong\mathbf Z/\ell\mathbf Z$. Hence $|H/\ell H|=\ell^N$. Comparing cardinalities with the previous step yields $\ell^r\leq\ell^N$, so $r\leq N$. This bounds every finite rationally independent family of actual endomorphisms, without yet choosing a basis of $E^0$.

source.place: Chapter I, Lemma 10.16 and proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.49; explicit finite-rank argument filling the transition to a rational basis.

proof.text: The possible sizes of finite rationally independent families in $E$ form a nonempty subset of $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so choose a family of maximal size. Its rational span contains every element of $E$: otherwise an element outside that span could be appended to obtain a larger independent family. Every element of $E^0$ is a finite sum $\sum_j a_j\otimes q_j=\sum_j q_j(a_j\otimes1)$ with $a_j\in E$ and $q_j\in\mathbf Q$; hence the family spans $E^0$ as well. For this finite-dimensional $V=E^0$, the subgroup $\Lambda=E\cap V$ in steps 3–4 is all of $E$. Their conclusion proves that $\operatorname{End}_k(C)$ is a free abelian group of finite rank for every positive-dimensional $k$-simple $C$. This is where the finite rational basis is first chosen.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.49, final sentence for simple varieties; the preceding rank bound makes that choice legitimate.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-simple-isogeny-decomposition], choose finite products $P=\prod_i A_i$, $Q=\prod_j B_j$ of positive-dimensional $k$-simple varieties and isogenies $p:P\to A$ and $q:B\to Q$; the latter is the quasi-inverse of an isogeny $Q\to B$. Choose quasi-inverses $p':A\to P$, $q':Q\to B$ and positive integers $n,m$ with $p\circ p'=[n]_A$ and $q'\circ q=[m]_B$. Send $f:A\to B$ to the finite matrix $(\pi_j\circ q\circ f\circ p\circ\iota_i)_{i,j}$ in $\prod_{i,j}\operatorname{Hom}_k(A_i,B_j)$, where $\iota_i$ inserts into one product factor and $\pi_j$ projects to one. This is an additive map. A group homomorphism out of a finite product is the sum of its restrictions to the factors, since the identity of the product is $\sum_i\iota_i\pi_i$. Thus a zero matrix means $qfp=0$. Composing gives $0=q'(qfp)p'=(q' q)f(pp')=[m]_B\circ f\circ[n]_A=mn f$, since a group homomorphism commutes with integer multiplication. Thus $f=0$ by the torsion-freeness proved in step 2. This proves injectivity, also for empty products.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.50, reduction to simple factors; quasi-inverse identities as in Remark 8.6.

proof.text: For each pair $A_i,B_j$, if there is no nonzero homomorphism, its Hom group is zero. Otherwise choose one $h:A_i\to B_j$; [lem-sfb-simple-isogeny-decomposition] makes it an isogeny, with quasi-inverse $v:B_j\to A_i$ and $hv=[t]_{B_j}$ for some $t>0$. The map $f\mapsto vf$ embeds $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A_i,B_j)$ into $\operatorname{End}_k(A_i)$: if $vf=0$, then $tf=hvf=0$, so $f=0$ by step 2. Each latter endomorphism group has a finite integer basis by step 6. Consequently [lem-weil-subgroup-finite-free-abelian-group-free] makes each simple-factor Hom group finite free. The finite product of these groups has the finite basis formed by inserting each factor's basis into its own coordinate, with other coordinates zero. Applying the same subgroup result to the injection in step 7 now proves that $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)$ has a finite integer basis.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Theorem 10.15, printed p.50, the embeddings $\operatorname{Hom}(A_i,B_j)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}(A_i)$ and the finite-product conclusion.

proof.text: Specialize the preceding conclusion to $B=A$. On $\operatorname{End}_k(A)$ define multiplication by $fg=f\circ g$. Associativity of morphism composition gives $(fg)h=f(gh)$; its identity laws give $\mathrm{id}_Af=f=f\mathrm{id}_A$. Additivity of composition from step 1 gives both distributive laws: $f(g+h)=fg+fh$ and $(f+g)h=fh+gh$. Together with the pointwise abelian-group law these are the unital associative ring axioms. Its additive group has the finite basis already obtained, and its multiplicative identity is exactly $\mathrm{id}_A$. For the zero abelian variety the additive group and ring each have one element; its empty basis and $1=0=\mathrm{id}_A$ satisfy the same assertion.

source.place: Chapter I, §10, printed pp.42–43, endomorphism-ring convention; Theorem 10.15 for its additive group.

proof_origin.place: Chapter I, proof of Theorem 10.15, printed pp.49–50; finite-rank transition expanded using saturation modulo ell before choosing a rational basis.

lean.statement: theorem abelianVariety_hom_finite_free {k : Type u} [Field k] (A B : Over (Spec (.of k))) [GrpObj A] [GrpObj B] [IsAbelianVariety A] [IsAbelianVariety B] : (∃ n : ℕ, Nonempty (Module.Basis (Fin n) ℤ (abelianVarietyHom A B))) ∧ ∃ r : Ring (abelianVarietyHom A A), r.toAddCommGroup = Additive.addCommGroup ∧ (∀ f g : abelianVarietyHom A A, (r.mul f g).val = g.val ≫ f.val) ∧ r.one.val = 𝟙 A ∧ ∃ n : ℕ, Nonempty (Module.Basis (Fin n) ℤ (abelianVarietyHom A A))
